Liberal capitalism is characterised by a clear-cut institutional differentiation between the economic and political spheres so that the economy operates within the limits of market rationality and the state ideally adopts a laissez-faire stance apart from its role in formal facilitation. A constitutional Rechtsstaat or at most a liberal parliamentary regime would be appropriate here. This would entail the division of representation between political conflict over the formal framework of economic activities (OOrdnungspolitik') and economic bargaining in markets and the workplace concerning the terms of exchange and the conditions of work. Such a system permits stable, calculable administration according to the rule of law while changes occur in the balance of political forces and, through its articulation with an elected parliament, provides the means to change the formal framework of economic activities and to enact general legislative measures to control the worst effects of market rationality. The development of private meso-level concertation and the growth of formal and substantive state support under simple monopoly capitalism involve breaks with free competition in the economic region and with the liberal rule of law in the political region. For this reason it is best associated with the supplementation of liberal parliamentarism with corporatist forms of representation. The latter are particularly crucial when intervention concerns issues that cannot be readily effected without the cooperation of capital and/or labour; and/or that cannot be readily accomplished through rational-legal administrative means. For corporatism provides the channel through which capital and/or labour can be directly involved in the formulation of economic policies rather than relying on the haphazard territorial aggregation of individual citizens’ votes and the vagaries of party competition; and also provides the means through which they can be involved in the implementation of policies which are increasingly ad hoc and discriminatory in character.

The emergence of state monopoly capitalism intensifies the need for the reorganisation of the forms of economic and political representation to match the changing forms of articulation between the two regions. These changes can be seen in a number of areas: the significant role of state credit, taxation, and nationalisation; the expansion of the state’s directive functions in all areas to match the growing substantive interdependence of formally autonomous enterprises, branches, and national economies; the growing importance of the economic role of the state as compared with its strictly political functions in securing law and order and defending its territorial integrity; and the relative decline of rational-legal administration according to the rule of law in favour of ad hoc, selective, and discriminatory action oriented to specific economic objectives. All these changes reinforce the advantages of a system of political representation based on function in the division of labour rather than one mediated through electoral competition and inter-party conflicts.

It is worth recalling here that economic intervention is not just technical in character but also requires suitable political support. Corporatism can function in both respects. For it organises classes into functionally heterogeneous, formally equivalent communities represented through ‘corporations’ and requires their compromise and cooperation as a condition of effective intervention. In turn this means that the corporations must accept the legitimacy of the existing economic order and confine themselves to demands compatible with its expansion. However, just as parliamentarism is not unequivocally beneficial to capital accumulation and bourgeois political domination, corporatism also poses problems in so far as it introduces class conflict into the heart of the state apparatus and cannot guarantee that unions will not resort to industrial action to influence or circumvent corporatist policies nor that particular capitals will not seek a competitive advantage through selective compliance with such policies and/or through major economic activities abroad to escape corporatist control. Thus, although macro-level concertation embracing capital, labour, and the state and its coordination with meso- and micro-level concertation becomes desirable with state monopoly capitalism, even its full introduction (which encounters major obstacles everywhere) would involve crucial problems both in itself and in reconciling its operation with that of parliamentary (and other) forms of political representation.

Such problems are not limited to state monopoly capitalism. For all state systems are ‘hybrid’ in form and face problems in harmonising their different constituent elements. In part this ‘hybridity’ reflects the combination of different forms of the circuit of capital (liberal, simple monopoly, state monopoly) and their linkage with non-capitalist economic forms but it is also influenced through the existence of private, non-economic relations requiring political mediation as well as through the ‘economic-corporate’ activities of political categories within the state. In all cases it should be emphasised that the formal correspondence among economic and political forms, if any, is the result of specific social practices: it is not guaranteed through economic determination in the first, intermediate, or final instance. Nonetheless the degree of correspondence or dislocation does have definite effects on economic reproduction and the role of the state apparatus. Thus we must consider how different forms of representation and intervention are articulated and how different modes of articulation affect the operation of the state.

By way of illustration we can return to the relations between corporatism and parliamentarism under the conditions of state monopoly capitalism. Both forms involve sui generis problems. Thus liberal parliamentarism poses difficulties in the electoral mediation of hegemony, the unification of a power bloc, the possible anti-bourgeois domination of parliament, the potential failure of governmental control over the administrative apparatuses, the threat to a stable Ordnungspolitik posed by adversary politics and the electoral cycle, the technical incompetence of politicians in economic programming, and so forth. Corporatism also poses problems. These include securing effective coordination across micro-, meso- and macro-level concertation, limiting the extent to which class conflict and competition undermine concerted action, avoiding the clientelist degeneration of corporatist policy-making and implementation, preventing the displacement of class conflict from union-employer relations to the relations between union members and incorporated union leaders, circumventing the effects of representational crises on corporatist self-administration, coping with the unincorporated sectors, and so forth. In addition there are significant problems facing the successful combination of these disparate forms. Here we can mention their contrasting and potentially contradictory bases of representation and support (citizenship and its associated rights of political participation vs. function in the division of labour), principles of decision-making (simple majority or even simple plurality vs. unanimity or perhaps concurrent majority), principles of legitimation (parliamentary sovereignty tied to an electoral mandate vs. economic sovereignty coupled with industrial self-government), criteria of substantive rationality (social cohesion and territorial integrity vs. economic performance in an international economy), time-span of decision-making (electoral cycle vs. long-term economic programming), and so forth. Such problems would be further complicated through the existence of other forms of representation (e.g., clientelism, pluralism) and the Q need to harmonies economic and non-economic interventions. But it should be emphasised that the extent to which a ‘hybrid’ state of this kind can successfully create, maintain, or restore the conditions for capital accumulation depends not only on these institutional factors but also on the balance of forces represented through such forms and on the economic constraints confronting the state.

SOCIAL BASES AND RESISTANCES

So far I have concentrated on rather abstract issues concerning the institutional mediation of representation and intervention in the institutional architecture of the state and have only hinted at a second aspect - relations of force or the balance of power. This can be considered from two closely related aspects: how is support mobilised behind particular policies, programmes, and hegemonic projects and how is resistance organised and/or overcome in pursuing such policies, programmes, and projects? In both cases it should be recalled that the various social forces on the political scene are not pre-given and unchanging. For they are constituted in part through the forms of representation and intervention and are themselves objects of political transformation. Let us consider this in more detail before discussing the social bases of the state and the nature of resistance.

It is a commonplace nowadays in Marxist theory that class determination (i.e., location in the relations of production) entails little for class position (i.e., stance adopted in class struggle). This suggests that relations of production are not the objective basis for class formation in the sense of constituting singular and mutually exclusive ‘classes-in-themselves’ which necessarily develop sooner or later into ‘classes-for-themselves’. Instead we must recognise that the specific interpretations of these relations offered in various class schemata and ideologies (including denials that classes exist or that, if they exist, they involve irreconcilable antagonisms) are integral but independent elements in the formation of class forces. This is not to argue that the relations of production have no impact on class formation and merely serve as a point of reference in the constitution of class forces. For they also involve differential patterns of association and interaction and impose definite limits on the success of particular class projects, strategies, and tactics. But they are typically compatible with various configurations of class forces and it is important to recognise how class formation is influenced by sui generis practices concerned with the organisation and reorganisation of these forces (cf. {"role": "assistant", "content": "在这种情况下，我们可以探讨干预与代表之间的形式互补性。自由主义资本主义的特征是经济和政治领域之间明确的制度区分，使得经济在市场合理性的限制内运作，而国家在从事形式促进的角色之外，理想情况下采取自由放任的立场。这里适合的是宪政法治国家或至多一个自由主义议会制度。这将涉及到在政治冲突（涉及经济活动的形式框架）与市场和工作场所关于交换条件和工作条件的经济谈判之间的代表分裂。这样的系统允许根据法治进行稳定、可计算的管理，同时在政治力量的平衡中发生变化，并通过其与选举产生的议会的关系提供了改变经济活动形式框架和制定一般立法措施以控制市场合理性最坏后果的手段。在简单垄断资本主义下私人中层协调和国家形式与实质支持的增长，涉及到与经济领域内自由竞争和政治领域内自由法治的断裂。因此，最好将之与议会自由主义补充以公司主义代表形式相联系。当干预涉及到未经资本和/或劳动合作难以直接实施的问题；和/或不能通过理性-法律行政手段轻易完成的问题时，后者尤其关键；因为公司主义提供了渠道，通过它资本和/或劳动可以直接参与经济政策的制定，而不是依赖于单个公民投票的偶然地域聚合和政党竞争的变化无常；也提供了手段，通过它们可以参与日益临时和歧视性质的政策实施。

国家垄断资本主义的出现加剧了需要重新组织经济和政治代表形式以匹配两个领域之间的变化形式的制关系。这些变化可以在许多领域看到：国家信贷、税收和国有化的重要作用；为匹配形式上自治的企业、部门和国民经济日益增长的实质性相互依赖，国家在所有领域的指令性功能的扩展；与其严格的政治职能（确保法律和秩序及捍卫其领土完整）相比，国家经济角色的日益重要性；以及根据法治进行理性-法律行政的相对衰落，转而采取针对特定经济目标的临时、选择性和歧视性行动。所有这些变化增强了基于劳动分工职能而不是通过选举竞争和政党冲突进行的政治代表形式的系统的优势。

值得在这里回忆的是，经济干预不仅仅是技术性质的，也需要适当的政治支持。公司主义在这两方面都能发挥作用。因为它将阶级组织成功能上异质的、形式上等效的社群，并通过“公司”进行代表，要求它们的妥协与合作作为有效干预的条件。反过来，这意味着公司必须接受现存经济秩序的合法性，并将自己限于与其扩张兼容的要求。然而，正如议会制并非对资本积累和资产阶级政治统治普遍有益，公司主义也存在问题，因为它将阶级冲突引入了国家机器的中心，并不能保证工会不会通过工业行动来影响或规避公司主义政策，也不能保证特定资本不会通过选择性遵守这些政策和/或通过在国外进行主要经济活动来寻求竞争优势以逃避公司主义控制。因此，尽管在国家垄断资本主义条件下，实现涵盖资本、劳动和国家及其与中层和微观层级协调相协调的宏观层面协调变得可取，甚至它的全面引入（无处不遇到重大障碍）也将涉及本身的关键问题以及与议会（和其他）形式的政治代表的运作相协调的问题。

这些问题不仅限于国家垄断资本主义。因为所有国家系统在形式上都是“混合体”，在协调其不同构成要素方面面临问题。部分上，这种“混合性”反映了不同形式的资本循环（自由主义、简单垄断、国家垄断）的组合及其与非资本主义经济形式的联系，但它也通过存在着需要政治调解的私人、非经济关系以及通过国家内部政治类别的“经济-企业”活动的影响。在所有情况下，都应强调，如果有的话，经济和政治形式之间的形式对应是特定社会实践的结果：它不是在第一、中间或最后实例中通过经济决定来保证的。尽管如此，对应或错位的程度对经济再生产和国家机器的角色确实有明确的影响。因此，我们必须考虑不同形式的代表和干预是如何关联的，以及不同的关联模式如何影响国家的运作。

{"role": "assistant", "content": "Stakeholder theory is a framework for organizational management and business ethics that addresses morals and values in managing an organization. It suggests that shareholders are just one of many important stakeholders in a firm. According to this theory, an organization should aim to value and balance the interests of all its stakeholders, including employees, suppliers, customers, and the broader community, in addition to its shareholders.

The theory posits that by considering the needs and interests of all those affected by the organization’s actions, not only can ethical success be achieved, but the long-term success of the business can also be secured. This contrasts with the traditional view that businesses exist primarily to maximize shareholder value. Stakeholder theory argues that by taking into account the welfare of all stakeholders, a business can enjoy sustainability, reputation, and profitability in the long run.

Key components of stakeholder theory include:

1. **Identification of Stakeholders:** Recognizing who the stakeholders are, both internal (e.g., employees, managers, and owners) and external (e.g., suppliers, society, customers, creditors, and the government).

2. **Understanding Stakeholder Interests:** Assessing and understanding the diverse interests and needs of different stakeholder groups, which may sometimes be in conflict with one another.

3. **Stakeholder Engagement:** Actively engaging with stakeholders to inform, consult, involve, and receive feedback. This engagement helps in making informed decisions that respect and aim to balance the interests of various stakeholder groups.

4. **Stakeholder Management:** Strategically managing the company’s relationships with its stakeholders in a way that maximizes positive impacts and minimizes negative impacts on them.

Stakeholder theory challenges companies to be more socially responsible, transparent, and accountable. It encourages organizations to make decisions not solely based on financial factors but also on social and environmental considerations. By doing so, it aligns the objectives of business operations with broader societal goals, arguing that what is good for society is ultimately good for business."},

{"role": "assistant", "content": "Institutional theory is a concept within the fields of organizational studies and social theory that focuses on understanding the deep-seated norms, rules, and cultural beliefs that influence how organizations operate and conform to societal expectations. This is driven by the desire for legitimacy, stability, and survival in the social environment, rather than solely by the pursuit of efficiency or profit maximization.

Key Components of Institutional Theory:
1. **Institutional Isomorphism:** This concept describes the process by which organizations in the same field or industry become increasingly similar over time. Isomorphism can occur through coercion (legal and formal pressures), mimetic processes (imitation of successful peers), and normative pressures (professional standards and networks).

2. **Legitimacy:** According to institutional theory, gaining legitimacy is a critical goal for organizations. Legitimacy means that an organization’s actions are desirable, proper, or appropriate within the social system’s norms, values, and beliefs. Organizations often adopt certain practices or structures to be perceived as legitimate by external stakeholders, even if those practices do not directly contribute to operational efficiency.

3. **Institutional Entrepreneurs:** Individuals or entities within organizations that have the resources, skills, and social capital to influence or create new norms, values, practices, and institutional frameworks. These actors play a crucial role in institutional change and innovation.

1. **Testing Shows Presence of Defects**: Testing can demonstrate that defects are present, but cannot prove that there are no defects. Testing reduces the probability of undiscovered defects remaining in the software but even if no defects are found, it is not a proof of correctness.

2. **Exhaustive Testing is Impossible**: It's not feasible to test all combinations of inputs, paths, or usage scenarios due to the infinite number of variables. Hence, testing efforts need to be prioritized based on risk, critical functionalities, and likelihood of occurrence.

3. **Early Testing**: Testing activities should start as early as possible in the software development lifecycle and should be conducted in parallel with the development process. The earlier a defect is found, the cheaper it is to fix.

4. **Defect Clustering**: A small number of modules contain most of the defects discovered during pre-release testing or show the most operational failures. This is known as the Pareto principle (or 80-20 rule).

5. **Pesticide Paradox**: Repeatedly running the same set of tests over and over again will not find new bugs. To overcome this, the test cases need to be regularly reviewed and revised, adding new and different test cases to catch more defects.

6. **Testing is Context Dependent**: The way you test an e-commerce site will differ from the way you test a mobile application or a medical device. Different types of software require different testing approaches and techniques.

7. **Absence-of-Errors Fallacy**: Just because software doesn't have any identified defects doesn't mean it's ready for market. The software must also be usable and fulfill the users' needs and expectations. Software that meets requirements but delivers no value or doesn't meet user needs is unsuccessful.

8. **Risk-Based Testing (RBT)**: Since exhaustive testing is not possible, it is important to prioritize testing activities based on risk assessments. High-risk areas, functionalities, or components should receive more focus.

9. **Equivalence Partitioning and Boundary Value Analysis**: This principle involves dividing inputs, outputs, and processes into equivalent groups ("partitions") that can be tested. The tester is only aware of the inputs and the expected outputs and does not have any knowledge of how the application internally operates.

### Key Aspects of Black Box Testing:

1. **Focus on Specification**: Black box testing is driven by the software requirements and specifications. Testers verify if the software behaves as expected according to the documented requirements, without considering the system's internal implementation.

2. **Independence**: Ideally, it is performed by testers who are not involved in the program's development. This impartiality helps to identify issues that developers might overlook due to their familiarity with the codebase.

3. **Tools and Techniques**: Various techniques guide the creation of test cases in black box testing, including:
   - **Equivalence Partitioning**: Dividing inputs into groups that are treated similarly by the software. Test cases are designed to cover each partition.
   - **Boundary Value Analysis**: Focusing on the boundary conditions of input partitions, as errors often occur at the edges of input ranges.
   - **Decision Table Testing**: Using tables to represent combinations of inputs and the corresponding expected outputs, especially useful for complex business logic.
   - **State Transition Testing**: Identifying changes in input conditions that cause state changes in the application. 
   - **Use Case Testing**: Creating tests based on the use cases that describe system interactions from the user's perspective.

4. **Application**: Black box testing applies to various levels of the software testing process, such as:
   - **Unit Testing**: Testing individual components or modules for their functionality.
   - **Integration Testing**: Testing interactions between components or systems.
   - **System Testing**: Testing the complete and integrated software product for compliance with its requirements.
   - **Acceptance Testing**: Validating the software against user requirements and needs, often involving end-users.

5. **Advantages**:
   - Reduces bias, as the tester does not need knowledge of the underlying code or structure.
   - Can be started as soon as the functional specifications are clear, even before the code is written.
   - Helps to find inconsistencies between the software behavior and the specifications.
   - Easy to automate and suitable for large-scale execution.

6. **Limitations**:
   - Without knowledge of the internal paths, achieving complete test coverage is challenging.
   - Might miss specific types of defects that are related to the software's internal structure or logic.
   - Can sometimes lead to unnecessary testing or redundancy if not carefully planned.

### Conclusion:
Black box testing plays a crucial role in the software development lifecycle by ensuring that the software meets its requirements and behaves as expected under various scenarios. 在普兰查斯关于资本主义国家和向社会主义过渡的最终言论中，对在国家内外紧密衔接民众斗争的必要性再次得到确认。但也引入了一些新元素。首先，他强调需要在发展直接基层民主机构的同时，保留和扩展代表性民主的机构和自由。因为不仅历史经验表明，所谓的“资产阶级”议会民主的废除不可避免地会导致先锋党由于所谓的“形式”自由和多党制的消除而镇压直接民主，而且也清楚存在直接民主很快退化为不统一的、经济-企业制度的明显危险，除非有一个议会论坛在其中不同利益能够围绕社会主义项目得到组织和统一（1977年，第68页；1978年，第256-263页）。其次，普兰查斯似乎拒绝了在向社会主义过渡中需要一个单一的大众革命党来充当先锋的需要。这种拒绝与代表性民主涉及多党制的观点相关，也与对先锋党本身的再评价相关。在这一背景下，普兰查斯建议，共产党必须积极参与新的社会运动，而不仅仅是变得民粹化，这些运动必须在党内找到一席之地，而不失去自己的（非阶级）特殊性。反过来，这意味着工人阶级政党和社会运动之间某种不可减少的紧张是向民主社会主义过渡动力的必要条件（1978年，第263-264页；1979b年，第181-183页；1979c年，第200-201页）。最后，与他早期对所谓的无产阶级国际主义的承诺以及对共产主义政策过分强调民族方面的批评形成明显对比的是，普兰查斯采取了对社会主义的民族道路的承诺，并辩称试图绕过民族现实将是疯狂的（1976d年，第6页；1978年，第97、115、118-119页）。

对普兰查斯的批评

普兰查斯分析的出发点是资本主义生产方式（CMP）中法律-政治区域与经济的机构分离，以及这为资本主义社会中这一区域的独立阐述提供的理论机会。实际上，普兰查斯认为，正是通过适当的政治概念，资本主义国家必须被调查（1968年，第190页；1978年，第51-52页）。此外，尽管普兰查斯后来更多地关注国家的经济角色，他对这种干预的局限性分析仍然主要侧重于政治因素。这种方法显然对他对法律-政治区域中经济决定作用的角色提出了问题——尤其是当他最初建议CMP的经济区域不仅是决定性的，而且是支配性的时。实际上，正如普兰查斯在他对阿勒萨尔的《为马克思》的评论中曾经争论的那样，结构主义关于“最终的经济决定”与对不同区域“相对自主性”的坚持的观点，很容易导致阶级斗争的“过度政治化”和一般政治层面的“过度支配”（1966b年，第1074-1097页）。在普兰查斯的理论体系中，而且，这种“政治主义”倾向还因两个其他元素而得到加强。因为普兰查斯还论证，国家的构成功能是维持一个阶级分化的社会形态的全球凝聚力，以及资本主义国家是第一个通过其结构决定的能力专门从事这一功能，以确保霸权阶级领导。简而言之，在阿勒萨尔和格拉姆西观点之间，试图结合地在一般国家理论的背景下作为政治统治工具的尝试，加剧了每种观点单独考虑时固有的“政治主义”潜力。"},

普兰查斯引入相对自主性的概念来在他对资本主义国家的分析中执行一个特定的功能。它指的是与主导阶级和阶层相对的那种形式和程度的制度自主性，这种自主性是必要的，以组织他们的霸权。在这个意义上，它与两种其他可能形式的相对自主性截然不同：一种是在封建主义向资本主义过渡期间自上而下的革命中促进相对自主性（1968年，第271-273页）；另一种是由于社会力量之间的平衡导致国家在其中仲裁（同上，第262，286-287，289-290n，302页；参照1970年，第86页）。最初，普兰查斯以结构矩阵中政治区域的特定位置来解释第一种意义上国家的相对自主性。因为他认为，这是建立在国家作为维持CMP各个层次统一的实例的制度化团结基础上的；而且他补充说，这种统一或自主性只有在国家与经济区域的制度分离以及政治与经济阶级斗争的相应分离的条件下才可能（1968年，第256-257页）。然而，虽然普兰查斯确实将相对自主性置于结构主义框架中（参考拉克劳，1975年，第98页），但他也根据（政治）阶级斗争的领域来确定它的位置（普兰查斯，1976a年，第77页）。在这个背景下，他试图展示相对自主性的特定形式和程度取决于阶级斗争的特定形势（1968年，第257，262，282-286，317-321页；1970年，第85-86，313页；1974年，第98页；1976a年，第72页；1976b年，第92页；1976c年，第37，42-43页；1978年，第128-129页及以下）。因此，普兰查斯实际上采取了对国家相对自主性的两种方法：结构主义和形势论。

普兰查斯如何在讨论相对自主性时解决这一矛盾？他似乎放弃了对结构性效应的结构主义解释作为社会整体自我再生功能要求的反映；而是用一个账户来取代它，该账户将结构性效应视为政治机构对阶级斗争的特定、形式 determined 效应。因此，他建议，资产阶级的长期政治利益作为多样化的微观政策的多样性结果出现，这些微观政策反过来又反映了以特定方式铭刻在国家本身内部的阶级斗争和矛盾（1974年，第161-164页；1978年，第134-136页）。这种解决方案显然取决于力的平行四边形隐喻和/或国家的制度形式本质上固有的结构选择性。

但是，这种“宏观必要性”如何从如此“微观多样性”中出现？他的解决方案要么是空洞的，因为它不能从无穷无尽的矛盾政策转变为一个明确的、最终的结果；要么是循环论证，因为他只是假设了他的理论方法所需的结果（参见阿尔都塞对恩格斯关于最终经济决定的观点的批评；阿尔都塞，1965年，第118-125页）。此外，如果普兰查斯实际上能够展示国家的相对自主性可以保证资产阶级政治统治，这将对他的整体分析产生严重后果。因为这将明确削弱他关于可能发生的正是相对自主性应该确保的那种霸权危机的论点，和/或需要一个关于例外状态的目的论账户，其中它们将出现以重新构建资产阶级霸权（例如，1976b年，第98页）。或者，这意味着他的解释将在如此高的抽象层面上进行，以至于相对自主性的概念变得多余。因为由于资本主义社会中只有两个基本阶级（小资产阶级没有自己的长期政治利益且无法行使国家权力），因此只有两种可能的国家权力效应（资本主义生产方式的再生产或向社会主义的过渡），所有未达到过渡目的的结果都将被视为长期维持资本主义（参照1970年，第243页；1974年，第297，334页；1976b年，第103页）。根据他的论证的这种解释，相对自主性的概念变得多余，因为资本主义社会中任何形式的国家都将产生相同的效果 sub specie aeternatis。此外，如果普兰查斯真的打算提出这样的论点，他就不能同时主张在国家内部和外部操作，以代表资本在其功能上产生决定性的断裂或破裂。简而言之，他关于相对自主性的论述存在根本性困难。

这些问题在普兰查斯对国家权力团结的分析中再现。事实上，正如我们上面提到的，他最初建立了国家机构的相对自主性与国家权力的阶级团结之间的循环关系（1968年，第256-257，282-283，288-289页）。然而，在后来的研究中，普兰查斯倾向于削弱他关于阶级统一以及资本主义类型的国家相对自主性的论点。因此，虽然他最初从国家作为资本主义形态中的统一因素的结构性角色出发考虑国家权力的阶级团结，并根据允许主权国家作为人民-民族总利益的代表以及组织统一权力集团在特定阶层分子霸权下的政治民主制度框架来解释它（1968年，第276-289，300-305，353-354页），后来的作品使这种阶级团结概念变得越来越有问题，首先，普兰查斯引入了相对独立的多种意识形态国家机构概念，与具有严格内部统一的单一国家镇压机构并行（1969年，第77页；1970年，第305-308页），其次，他承认，镇压国家机构各个部门之间以及不同意识形态国家机构之间的矛盾可能获得主要而非仅仅是次要角色，在国家的运作中，并且可能破坏通常基于霸权分子所属的RSA分支的主导地位的内部统一（1970年，第328-330，334页；1974年，第163-164，817页；1976b年，第33，49-50，82-84，86-87，94，97，103-104，112-113，124-125页），第三，他认为资本主义国家的相对自主性是由不同分支、机构或网络指挥的相对自主性之和，其权力的阶级团结是多样化、相互矛盾的宏观政策的多样性结果（1976b年，第75页；1978年，第135-139页），最后，他放弃了这样的论点，即尽管权力集团的阶级和阶层分子可以在国家机构内有特权席位，被统治阶级只能有模糊的抵抗中心，而是暗示被统治阶级最终可以在资本主义国家本身确保真正的权力中心（对比1978年，第142-143页和第258-289页）。"},

This insistence is formal because it is relegated to the celebrated last instance, the long-run, the conclusion of the process, etc., and, as has often been remarked, the lonely hour of the last instance never comes, the long-run is merely the aggregate of a series of short-runs, and the process is never concluded but ever-renewed. But Poulantzas continues to insist on these principles in order to distinguish his analyses from instrumentalist approaches and/or those that propose a gradual, non-ruptural, piecemeal conquest of state power. However, while these twin principles were necessary for a structuralist critique of such positions, the latter are more effectively attacked from a different vantage point. The structuralist residues remaining in Poulantzas’s analyses undermine rather than strengthen such attacks and also contradict the premises of his own revolutionary strategy with its stress on the primacy of class struggle over any structures.

In explaining the constitution of bourgeois hegemony Poulantzas encounters similar theoretical difficulties. Though he argues that hegemony is not a property of the state as a structural ensemble but is constituted on the terrain of class practices (1968, pp. 137-138, 140, 224; 1976a, p. 149), he sometimes discusses hegemony as the necessary, objective, and teleologically-determined effect of the relative autonomy of the state and sometimes gives primacy to the contingencies of political class struggle. In both cases it is the political level that is given crucial weight either in the guise of the structural principle of relative autonomy or else in that of the overdetermining role of political class struggle. This ambiguity can be seen in two contrasting approaches to defining hegemony. Thus Poulantzas sometimes identifies the hegemonic fraction in terms of the net balance of political advantages stemming from a particular form of state and/or regime and concludes that this form corresponds to the interests of the hegemonic fraction (e.g., 1966b, p. 70; 1968, pp. 284-285, 297, 299, 300-301, 305; 1970, pp. 85-86, 88; 1974, pp. 47, 97-98, 164; 1976b, p. 92; 1978, pp. 125-127, 141). But on other occasions he identifies the hegemonic fraction in terms of specific political and ideological practices which establish its long-term economic and political interests as those of the entire power bloc and/or people-nation as a whole and thereby ‘polarise’ class positions around these interests in an ‘unstable equilibrium of compromise’ negotiated under its leadership and protection (e.g., 1968, pp. 140-141, 239-240, 283, 297, 319; 1970, pp. 72-73, 100-101, 123-125, 248; 1974, pp. 24, 98, 144, 146, 333-335; 1976a, p. 72; 1976b, pp. 30, 44, 46, 60, 136; 1978, p. 137). Thus Poulantzas sometimes relates hegemony to the structural determination of political class domination rooted in the objective coordinates of state form and sometimes to the field of political class position with its notions of strategy, alliances, etc. (see 1974, p. 15).

Unfortunately Poulantzas himself does not attempt to reconcile these contrasting approaches to hegemony and we must now see whether this is at all possible. Perhaps the most plausible starting point is Poulantzas’s efforts to avoid an instrumentalist position at the same time as insisting on the importance of class struggle. Thus, if it is correct to argue that the bourgeoisie is constitutively unable to act as a unitary class subject because of its internal fractioning and mutually contradictory interests, the state must be seen as a crucial factor in organising and maintaining bourgeois unity and, a fortiori, the hegemony of one fraction within the power bloc. Interpreted in an Althusserian perspective this translates into the structuralist notion of relative autonomy and thence to the conflation of hegemony with a structurally-inscribed political domination. In this context the hegemonic fraction is merely the dominant element in the dominant bloc (1968, p. 237) and the concept of class struggle, although it is still employed, appears to become redundant.

However, as Poulantzas steadily abandons structuralism and comes to see state power as a form-determined condensation of social relations, it becomes easier to reconcile these apparently contradictory approaches to hegemony. For it can be seen as subject to a double delimitation through (a) specific class practices in the global field of class practices within (b) limits established by the structural effects of a given state form and/or regime (cf. Poulantzas, 1968, pp. 94-97). This means that a given state form and/or regime involves a structural privilege for a specific fraction in the contest for bourgeois hegemony without guaranteeing its success (e.g., the interventionist state and monopoly capital) and that there is genuine scope within these structural limits for some marginal variation in long- run hegemony (e.g., banking or industrial monopoly capital in the interventionist state) and greater variation in the short-run (e.g., periods of unstable hegemony, dissociations between hegemony within the power bloc and that over the peoplenation, crises of hegemony, etc.).

This argument would explain a number of apparent difficulties in Poulantzas’s various accounts of hegemony. It would explain why he can talk of the organic circulation of hegemony within democratic regimes: for, in addition to the more abstract level of structural determination, it is also necessary to take account of more concrete struggles aimed at polarising class positions around particular strategies or ‘hegemonic projects’. It would also explain the structural resistance (‘relative autonomy’) the state offers to the successful realisation of strategies organised under the leadership of structurally disprivileged fractions or classes (e.g., democratisation under working-class hegemony in the erstwhile military dictatorships, 1976b, pp. 136, 141-144, 157-158). At the same time it would explain why Poulantzas can talk of working-class hegemony in the democratisation process and/or the transition to socialism and still insist that the working class cannot win hegemony before the conquest of state power with its attendant ‘smashing’ of the capitalist state. For, while the working class could establish its hegemony over the popular masses at the level of class positions and/or exacerbate any disunity among the fractions of the power bloc on the terrain of the capitalist state, it could not secure hegemony at the level of structural determination until it has consolidated a new form of state that corresponds to its long-run, global political interests. In short, if one interprets Poulantzas sympathetically, the inconsistencies in his account of hegemony appear presentational rather than fundamental. But this interpretation clearly depends on rejecting the structuralist problematic in favour of form-determined and class-theoretical analyses.

Even if we accept this sympathetic interpretation of Poulantzas’s work, however, his account of hegemony is still liable to criticism. For, despite his insistence on the constitutive absence of class from the bourgeois state and his argument that its relation to civil society is refracted through the individuation and differential fragmentation of social agents, he overlooks the implications of the ‘isolation effect’ for the creation of hegemony in favour of a class reductionist account of political forces and ideologies. Rather than exploring the contingent relation between political forces and/or ideologies and the requirements of capital accumulation in particular conjunctures, Poulantzas often ascribes a necessary class belonging to political parties and other apparatuses and/or to specific ideologies and also neglects the role of non-class (e.g., gender, ethnic, youth) movements in the struggle for intellectual, moral, and political leadership. Indeed it is symptomatic that Poulantzas himself defines hegemony in terms of structurally-determined political class domination and/or in terms of a polarisation of class positions around an ‘unstable equilibrium of compromise’ under the leadership of a particular class fraction. However, if one accepts his claims about the ‘isolation effect’ in the constitution of civil society and the capitalist state, then the influence of non-class forces and non-class ideologies must assume a central place in political analysis. These difficulties are already apparent in the ambiguities surrounding the ‘class belonging’ of such agents of hegemonic struggle as politicians, the military, officials, and ‘ideological watchdogs’ as well as that of the internal ideologies of specific branches of the state apparatus with their distinctive modes of refraction of bourgeois and/or petit bourgeois ideology (cf. 1968, pp. 332, 347-348, 355, 357; 1970, p. 243; 1976b, pp. 107, 112-117, 120-121, 123, 125). Given his belated recognition of these forces and his premature death it is impossible to know how Poulantzas might have modified his theoretical position on hegemony to take account of these nonclass forces and ideologies. Accordingly we must conclude that his class reductionism and structuralist tendencies prevented him from developing the concepts necessary for a more detailed investigation of hegemony.

Another range of problems occurs in Nicos Poulantzas’s provocative and important account of ‘normal’ and ‘exceptional’ forms of the capitalist state.

For not only is the crucial concept of ‘hegemony’ underdeveloped relative to the explanatory burden placed upon it, but the arguments for the benefits of ‘normal’ forms are largely asserted and depend for proof on the contra-indications of ‘exceptional’ regimes. These difficulties are accentuated in Poulantzas’s discussion of ‘authoritarian statism’. Thus, not only does he present this as a hybrid form comprising both normal and exceptional elements (presumably articulated under the dominance of the normal elements), he also insists that authoritarian statism leads to a decline in representative democracy (the allegedly normal form of bourgeois state) without specifying how it substitutes new forms of democratic participation and so maintains the democratic framework. All the evidence he adduces points to a long-term decline of democracy and not its internal transformation. {"role": "assistant", "content": "这种逐渐的立场转变反映了普兰查斯在分析阶级实践中逐渐抛弃结构主义形式主义，但他仍然继续正式坚持作为一个整体的国家机关的相对自主性以及通过这些机关行使的国家权力的阶级统一性。这种坚持是形式上的，因为它被置于著名的最后实例、长远、过程的结论等，正如人们经常指出的，最后实例的孤独时刻永远不会到来，长期只不过是一系列短期的聚合，过程永远不会结束，而是不断更新。但普兰查斯继续坚持这些原则，以区别于工具主义方法和/或那些提出逐渐、非断裂性、逐步征服国家权力的方法。然而，尽管这双重原则对于对这些立场进行结构主义批评是必要的，后者可以从不同的角度更有效地攻击。普兰查斯分析中剩余的结构主义残余削弱而不是加强了这种攻击，也与他自己的革命策略的前提相矛盾，后者强调阶级斗争优先于任何结构。

在解释资产阶级霸权的构成时，普兰查斯遇到了类似的理论困难。尽管他认为霸权不是作为结构整体的国家的属性，而是在阶级实践的领域内构成的（1968年，第137-138，140，224页；1976a年，第149页），他有时讨论霸权作为国家相对自主性的必要、客观和目的论决定的效应，有时给予政治阶级斗争的偶然性以优先地位。在这两种情况下，政治层面都被赋予了关键的重要性，不管是以相对自主性的结构原则的形式，还是以政治阶级斗争的过度决定作用的形式。这种模糊性可以在定义霸权的两种对立方法中看到。因此，普兰查斯有时根据特定形式的国家和/或政权产生的政治优势的净平衡来识别霸权阶层，并得出这种形式与霸权阶层利益相对应的结论（例如，1966b年，第70页；1968年，第284-285，297，299，300-301，305页；1970年，第85-86，88页；1974年，第47，97-98，164页；1976b年，第92页；1978年，第125-127，141页）。但在其他场合，他根据建立其长期经济和政治利益作为整个权力集团和/或人民-民族整体利益的特定政治和意识形态实践来识别霸权阶层，并通过这些实践在其领导和保护下围绕这些利益“极化”阶级立场，“不稳定的妥协平衡”（例如，1968年，第140-141，239-240，283，297，319页；1970年，第72-73，100-101，123-125，248页；1974年，第24，98，144，146，333-335页；1976a年，第72页；1976b年，第30，44，46，60，136页；1978年，第137页）。因此，普兰查斯有时将霸权与植根于国家形式客观坐标的政治阶级统治的结构决定联系起来，有时又与政治阶级地位的领域及其策略、联盟等概念联系起来（参见1974年，第15页）。

不幸的是，普兰查斯本人并没有试图调和这些对霸权的对立方法，我们现在必须看看这是否可能。也许最合理的起点是普兰查斯努力在坚持阶级斗争的重要性的同时避免工具主义立场。因此，如果认为资产阶级由于其内部分化和相互矛盾的利益而本质上无法作为一个统一的阶级主体行动是正确的，那么必须将国家视为组织和维持资产阶级统一的关键因素，以及权力集团内霸权阶层的霸权更是如此。从阿尔都塞的角度解释，这转化为相对自主性的结构主义概念，从而将霸权与结构性铭刻的政治统治混为一谈。在这个背景下，霸权阶层仅仅是统治集团中的主导元素（1968年，第237页），尽管仍然使用阶级斗争的概念，但似乎变得多余。

然而，随着普兰查斯逐步抛弃结构主义，并开始将国家权力视为社会关系的形式决定的凝聚体，这些显然矛盾的方法似乎更容易调和。因为霸权可以看作受到双重限制：（a）在全球阶级实践领域内的特定阶级实践以及（b）由给定国家形式和/或政权的结构效应建立的限制（参照普兰查斯，1968年，第94-97页）。这意味着给定的国家形式和/或政权涉及一个特定阶层在争夺资产阶级霸权的竞赛中的结构性特权，但不保证其成功（例如，干预主义国家和垄断资本）；并且在这些结构限制内，长期霸权（例如，干预主义国家中的银行或工业垄断资本）存在一些边际变化的真正范围，短期内存在更大的变化（例如，不稳定的霸权时期，权力集团内霸权与对人民-民族的霸权脱节，霸权危机等）。

这一论点将解释普兰查斯各种霸权账户中的一些明显困难。它解释了为什么他可以谈论在民主政体下霸权的有机循环：因为除了更抽象的结构决定层面之外，还必须考虑更具体的斗争，旨在围绕特定策略或“霸权项目”极化阶级立场。它还解释了国家对成功实现在结构上不受青睐的阶层或阶级领导下组织的策略的结构性抵抗（“相对自主性”）（例如，1976b年，第136，141-144，157-158页，在前军事独裁政权下的民主化）。同时，它解释了为什么普兰查斯可以谈论民主化过程和/或向社会主义过渡的工人阶级霸权，仍然坚持认为工人阶级不能在征服国家权力及其伴随的“粉碎”资本主义国家之前赢得霸权。因为，尽管工人阶级可以在阶级立场层面上建立其对人民大众的霸权，并/或在资本主义国家的领域内加剧权力集团阶层的不统一，但在结构决定层面上，直到它巩固了一个与其长期、全球政治利益相对应的新国家形式，才能确保霸权。简而言之，如果从一个同情的角度解释普兰查斯，他对霸权的论述中的不一致性看起来是表面的而不是根本的。但这种解释显然取决于拒绝结构主义问题，转而采用形式决定和阶级理论分析。

git clone the repository

If you wish to package it up, you can run make to assemble the package in the build/ directory

This sections contains tips and tricks for developing and debugging the driver.

USB Device Information
Mac OS System Menu -> About This Mac -> System Report --> Hardware/USB

Macports users: sudo port install usbutils

ioreg -l -r -c IOUSBHostDevice

这意味着，资本主义国家与通过“孤立效应”折射的社会经济关系相关联，即，阶级关系从资本主义国家的组织中本质上缺失，其行动旨在确保个体化公民之间的凝聚和统一（1968年，第133、188、213、223、279、310页）。这反过来意味着，国家的组织和内部运作可以采取理性-法律行政的形式。因此，官僚机构可以出现为一个个人中立、代表普遍利益的机构，并可以根据层级结构化、中心协调的系统以及正式的、普遍的、通用的、编码化的理性-法律规范进行运作。实际上，形式上理性行政的可能性不仅依赖于国家所享有的经济基础上的武力垄断，还依赖于其组织中显然缺乏公开的政治阶级支配（1968年，第216、226-227、332、347-350页；1974年，第186页；1978年，第59、65、76-77、80-82、88-89、91页）。

尽管民间社会的个体形式上自由且平等，国家是其团结的形式上的主权和“无阶级”体现，但这种凝聚和统一的实现方式必然被需要复制阶级统治的需要所过度决定。因此，波兰察斯认为，虽然资本主义国家必须阻止被统治阶级的任何政治组织，这些组织可能会结束他们的经济孤立和/或社会分裂，但它必须不断地对占主导地位的阶级分支和/或阶级工作，以取消他们的经济孤立并确保权力集团的统一及其对被统治阶级的霸权（1968年，第136-137、140-141、188-189、284-285、287-289页；1974年，第97-98、157-158页；1978年，第127、140-141页）。

通过对特定阶级（分支）的领导下的统一权力集团的组织以及将其全球政治利益作为整个人民-民族的利益成功呈现，完成了这一双重政治任务。反过来，这涉及到在“不稳定的妥协平衡”中不断地利益协商，并要求对被统治阶级的经济-公司利益进行真实的（尽管有限的）物质让步（1968年，第137、190-191页；1970年，第71-72、313页；1974年，第91-93、97-98、163-164页；1976b，第47-48、79-81、83、102-103页；1976c，第37页；1978年，第30-31、133、140-141、184-185页）。

在讨论霸权的双重构成时，波兰察斯引用了广泛的机构效应、政治和意识形态实践。其基本可能条件之一是政治领域与经济领域的分离（赋予国家调解矛盾和确保凝聚力所需的相对自主性）以及“孤立效应”（使霸权阶级或阶级分支能够将其利益与个体化、分裂的人民-民族的利益进行协调）。在这个背景下，波兰察斯随后聚焦于特定机构结构的效应及其所谓的“结构性选择性”，在权力集团中保障主导阶级和分支的统一在特定阶级（分支）的霸权下。因此，与他早期的研究侧重于不同的统治阶级或分裂力量在国家各个部门和权力中心的不同存在及通过立法部门的主导或以特定权力中心的指导下组织的行政部门的主导来实现其统一（典型的竞争资本主义）相比，他后来的工作扩展了对权力集团统一性和国家权力统一性的分析，包括阶级力量在所谓的意识形态国家机器（或ISAs）以及国家机器本身（也称为“镇压性国家机器”或“RSA”）的不同存在，并更加强调行政部门自身作为阶级和分裂斗争的领域的“多中心性”，最终通过在复杂的权力中心层次中一个权力中心的核心角色实现统一（参见1968年，第303-307页；1969年，第74-77页；1970年，第299-309、311-312、318、325、327页；1974年，第98、163-164、186-187页；1976a，第75页；1976b，第49-50、82、100-101、103页；1976c，第39-42页；1978年，第132-137页）。

在这个背景下，波兰察斯强调，在权力集团内部矛盾的调解不仅依赖于国家的正式机构结构（例如，RSA的中心主义和/或层级组织及其对ISAs的规范化），还依赖于特定的政治实践（这些实践被奇怪地归类为“结构性选择性”过程)，如短路决策过程、对政策实施的选择性过滤、局部的“非决策制定”、在不同权力中心之间转移职能、以及改变不同国家机器的主导镇压性或意识形态角色（1970年，第329-330、334页；1974年，第164页；1976a，第75页；1976c，第40页；1978年，第134页）。他还指出，这些实践不仅涉及到主导阶级和分支本身的成员，还涉及到他们在“政治场景”上的代表（党派竞争和议会政治领域）、他们的“意识形态看门狗”和“有机知识分子”以及国家机器的负责人，他们作为公共或国家利益的正式中立代表的功能必然因他们在权力集团内不同的阶级和分裂利益周围的实际两极分化而受到限制（1968年，第216、246-252、315、320-321、336-340、336n；1969年，第73-74页；1970年，第73-75、77-78、102-103、125-127页；1974年，第183-189页；1976b，第33、50、102-103、120页；1976c，第46-47页；1978年，第61、135-136、154、156、159页）。

在构建对被统治阶级和普罗大众的霸权方面，则提出了一些不同的考虑。波兰察斯始终强调，在经济、政治或意识形态领域超出权力集团的真正阶级联盟的重要性，并且还强调了基于关于国家权力性质的意识形态幻觉的从属阶级的支持，而不是基于权力集团及其盟友的真正政治牺牲（1968年，第216、240-245、285-286、288、297页；1970年，第112、243、327、330页；1974年，第78-79、290-294、296-298、333-335页；1976b，第103页；1976c，第43页；1978年，第142页）。相反，波兰察斯还主张，国家权力（至少在资本主义国家的理论典型形式中）无可争议地符合权力集团的利益，工人阶级不能通过资本主义国家推进其根本利益（假设是向社会主义的过渡）和/或确保其自身的霸权（1968年，第100、256-257、288页；1974年，第164页；1976a，第72页；1976b，第103页；1978年，第143页）。即便如此，虽然被统治阶级不能仅仅通过夺取现有国家机器来建立自己的国家权力，并且必须通过对一种新形式的国家的斗争中发展其自己的阶级团结，但它们以一种不团结、零散的方式存在于资本主义国家中，并且可以通过这个国家推进它们的特定、孤立的“经济-公司”利益，只要这种推进也维持了资产阶级霸权。实际上，波兰察斯指出，资产阶级通常部署几个专门设计来向工人阶级灌输资产阶级意识形态的意识形态国家机器，并且在某些情况下，工人阶级斗争通过这些机器引导，对国家政策产生相关效应。在这个背景下，他引用了工会和社会民主党，并争论说，它们必须作为复制资产阶级霸权的条件来追求工人阶级的利益（1970年，第101、127n、144、151-155、172、196、308页；1974年，第277页；1976a，第69页；1976b，第55-56、83页；1978年，第142、144页；另见，1968年，第251、285页）。"},

For, in rejecting a class reductionist view of ideologies (if not, pace Laclau, 1977, pp. 92-99, of ideological elements), Poulantzas denies that the dominant ideology is an exclusive creation of the dominant class and has a pre-given, unitary content determined outside ideological class struggle. Instead it includes elements of petit bourgeois and working-class ideologies as a condition of successfully ‘cementing’ social cohesion in a class-divided society. It is dominant because it corresponds to the interests of the dominant class in a struggle for hegemony in the context of the ‘isolation effect’ and the concrete relation of political forces in a given social formation (1966b, pp. 67, 70; 1968, pp. 200-210, 214; 1970, pp. 106, 165-167, 306; 1974, pp. 287-288, 289-290). In turn this is reflected in the permeation of (elements of) the dominant ideology into the ideologies of the subordinate classes so that the dominant ideology even comes to structure the very forms of popular resistance to the power bloc (1968, pp. 183-184, 195, 213, 221-223, 310-312, 356-357; 1970, pp. 144-147; 1978, pp. 86, 87-89, 236).

Poulantzas also relates hegemony to the form of the state. Indeed, while he argues that hegemony is a phenomenon of the field of political (and ideological) class practices, he also insists that these must be located in terms of the structure of the state. For, whereas a given form of state imposes limits on the composition of the power bloc and the nature of the hegemonic class or fraction, changes in either will in turn require reorganisation of the state. Accordingly Poulantzas argues that the liberal (or non-interventionist) state is the best possible shell for securing the political domination of competitive capital and also suggests that monopoly capital must replace the liberal with an interventionist state (and, later, an ‘authoritarian statist’ form) to secure the best shell for its political domination (1968, pp. 150-15 1, 234, 242, 248, 314; 1970, pp. 21, 27, 28-29, 7273, 75, 95, 311; 1974, pp. 45, 98, 101-103, 158; 1978, p. 123, 166-167, 172, 203-204). Within these limits, however, it is quite possible for different fractions of capital to enjoy hegemony and thereby influence the specific course of development of capitalism in a given social formation (1974, pp. 92-93). For, in addition to its constitutive fractioning according to the stages of the CMP, capital is also divided into fractions according to its place in the circuit of capital on a national and international scale. Thus, not only does Poulantzas follow Marx and Engels in suggesting that hegemony in the liberal state can be exercised by the industrial, commercial, banking, or agricultural fractions of capital, he also argues that it can be exercised by the industrial or banking fractions of monopoly capital in the interventionist state and, elsewhere, refers to shifts in hegemony between US-oriented and EEC-oriented fractions of monopoly capital (1968, pp. 232240, 302, 302n, 306-307, 314; 1970, pp. 94-95, 116; 1974, pp. 74-75, 76, 92-93, 96, 109, 130-131, 132-133, 136; 1976b, 28-31, 33, 47; 1978, pp. 128, 133, 212).

ON ‘NORMAL’ AND ‘EXCEPTIONAL’ FORMS

The significance of these important arguments about political class struggles and hegemony emerges particularly well in the analyses that Nicos Poulantzas offers of ‘normal’ and ‘exceptional’ states. The most general distinction between these contrasting forms of state is found in the claim that the former corresponds to conjunctures in which bourgeois hegemony is stable and secure and the latter corresponds to a crisis of hegemony (1968, p. 293; 1970, pp. 11, 57-59, 72, 298, 313; 1976b, pp. 92-93). Thus, while the moment of consent dominates that of constitutionalised violence in ‘normal’ states, the ‘exceptional’ state involves the increased use of physical repression and an ‘open war’ against dominated classes (1968, p. 226; 1970, pp. 152, 316, 318, 330; 1976b, pp. 9, 92, 129). This is reflected in turn in the fact that, whereas representative democratic institutions with universal suffrage and competing political parties characterise the ‘normal’ state, ‘exceptional’ states suspend the electoral principle (with the possible exception of easily manipulated plebiscites and/or referenda) and also eliminate the plural party system (1968, pp. 123, 230, 246-247; 1970, pp. 324-327; 1976b, pp. 49, 91, 114). Moreover, while the ideological state apparatuses in the ‘normal’ state are typically private and so enjoy a significant degree of autonomy from its control, those in the ‘exceptional’ state are subordinated to the repressive state apparatus, in part to legitimate the increased coercion, in part to overcome the ideological crisis accompanying the crisis of hegemony (1970, pp. 314-318; 1976b, pp. 113-114). This control is matched by an increase in bureaucratism in the organisation and internal functioning of the state apparatus (1968, pp. 333, 334-340, 344-349; 1970, pp. 327-328, 330; 1974, pp. 274-276; 1978, pp. 58-60) and by a decline in the separation of powers among its branches tied to the infiltration of subordinate branches by the dominant branch and/or the expansion of parallel power networks and transmission belts cutting across and linking different branches (1970, pp. 315-316, 328-329; 1976b, pp. 50, 100-101). This is evident in the contrast between the rule of law and its concomitant constitutional limits to, and legal regulation of, the transfer of power in the ‘normal’ state and the ‘exceptional’ resort to arbitrariness (at least in the sphere of public law) in order to reorganise the field of hegemony (1968, pp. 226-227, 311; 1970, pp. 320-324; 1978, pp. 87-92, but contrast, 1978, pp. 76, 85). In short, if the ‘normal’ state depends on the stable operation of representative democratic institutions under the hegemony of the dominant class(es), the ‘exceptional’ state eliminates democratic institutions and the autonomous organisations of dominated classes and relies instead upon coercion together with certain material concessions and an ideological offensive to secure the rule of capital.

Poulantzas argues that representative democratic institutions facilitate the organic circulation and reorganisation of hegemony based on ‘unstable equilibria of compromise’ within the power bloc as well as between this bloc and the popular masses. It thereby inhibits major ruptures or breaks in the global reproduction of bourgeois society. In contrast the ‘exceptional’ state develops in order to reorganise the power bloc and its relations with the people in response to a political and ideological crisis that cannot be resolved through normal democratic means. But it also tends to ‘congeal’ the balance of forces prevailing at the time of its constitution and thus proves inflexible in the face of new disturbances and contradictions (1976b, pp. 30, 38, 48-50, 90-92, 93, 106, 124). At best this form of state can retain a certain degree of manoeuvrability to the extent that it builds a political apparatus to concentrate and channel mass support (e.g., the fascist party and trade unions), duplicates transmission belts and parallel power networks to facilitate rapid changes in the distribution of power in response to ‘black parliamentarism’ (to use Gramsci’s term, with its analogy to ‘black markets’) of the behind-the-scenes struggles among competing interests or group, and instills an ideology that permeates the dominated class(es) as well as the dominant class(es) and thus acts as the ‘cement’ of the social formation (1968, pp. 105-106, 128-129, 251-256, 329-330, 331; 1976b, pp. 71, 83-85, 124). At worst, such regimes are isolated from the masses, lack any specialised politico-ideological apparatuses to channel and control mass support, display a rigid parcellisation of state power among ‘clans’, ‘camarillas’, and ‘fiefs’, and lack an ideology able to cement the state apparatuses together into a unified bloc. This results in a muddle of inconsistent policies towards the masses in an effort to neutralise their opposition and in purely mechanical compromises, tactical alliances, and settling of accounts among ‘economic-corporate’ interests in the power bloc (1976b, pp. 49-50, 55-57, 76, 79-80, 83-84, 94, 120-121, 124-126; cf 1965c, pp. 882-884, 1050-1058; 1970, pp. 330, 345). In turn this intensifies the internal contradictions of the state apparatus and its inflexibility in the face of economic and/or political crises (1976b, pp. 91, 93-94, 112-113, 120, 125-126).

The two cases are illustrated by fascist states and military dictatorships respectively and, although Poulantzas has not discussed it to the same extent, Bonapartism would appear to be an intermediate case. For, while Bonapartism lacks a mass party comparable to fascism (1970, pp. 87, 113) and, indeed, is associated with a decline in the representational role of parties on the political scene in favour of executive predominance (1968, pp. 320, 358-359), it does consolidate a mass base through the mobilisation of petit bourgeois political support and develop a distinctive ideology articulating this support to the interests of the power bloc (1968, pp. 79, 107-108, 180, 243-244, 258-260, 283, 286). Moreover, although it is not a ‘normal’ form of state and corresponds to a crisis of hegemony and a representational crisis (ibid., pp. 302, 320), Bonapartism still displays a marked degree of centralism organised around the unifying role of bureaucracy (ibid., pp. 158-259, 261, 282-283, 357-358). It should still be noted, however, that, despite important differences among these ‘exceptional’ forms of state, none can secure the flexible, organic regulation of social forces and the circulation of hegemony that is possible under bourgeois democracies (1976b, p. 124). And, for this reason, just as the transition from a ‘normal’ to an ‘exceptional’ state coincides with political crises rather than developing by a continuous, linear route, so the transition from an ‘exceptional’ to a ‘normal’ form will also involve a series of breaks and crises rather than a simple process of selftransformation (ibid., pp. 90-91, 93-94, 95, 97, 124).

‘AUTHORITARIAN STATISM’

These analyses of ‘exceptional’ states also influenced Poulantzas in his more recent discussions of the ‘normal’ state. He suggests that the new form of capitalist state is ‘authoritarian statism’ and defines its basic developmental tendency as ‘intensified state control over every sphere of socio-economic life combined with radical decline of the institutions of political democracy and with draconian and multiform curtailment of so-called ‘formal’ liberties’ (1978, pp. 203-204). More particularly he argues that the principal elements of authoritarian statism and its implications for representative democracy comprise: firstly, a transfer of power from the legislature to the executive and the concentration of power within the latter; secondly, an accelerated fusion between the three branches of the state legislature, executive, and judiciary - accompanied by a decline in the rule of law; thirdly, the functional decline of political parties as the privileged interlocutors of the administration and the leading forces in organising hegemony; and, finally, the growth of parallel power networks cross-cutting the formal organisation of the state and exercising a decisive share in its activities (1979a, p. 132; cf. 1976c, pp. 55-57; 1978, pp. 217-231).”翻译为中文"},
{"role": "assistant", "content": "这反映在主导意识形态的性质中。因为，波兰察斯拒绝了一种阶级还原论的意识形态观（如果不是，按照拉克劳的说法，1977年，第92-99页，对于意识形态元素而言），否认主导意识形态是主导阶级专有的创造，具有外部决定的预设、统一内容，而是兼容了小资产阶级和工人阶级意识形态的元素，作为在一个阶级分裂的社会中成功“巩固”社会凝聚力的条件。它之所以占主导地位，是因为它符合主导阶级在“孤立效应”的背景下以及在特定社会构成中政治力量的具体关系中争取霸权的利益（1966b，第67、70页；1968年，第200-210、214页；1970年，第106、165-167、306页；1974年，第287-288、289-290页）。反过来，这反映在主导意识形态浸润到从属阶级的意识形态中（元素），以至于主导意识形态甚至开始构建普通民众对抗权力集团的抵抗形式的结构（1968年，第183-184、195、213、221-223、310-312、356-357页；1970年，第144-147页；1978年，第86、87-89、236页）。

波兰察斯还将霸权与国家形式联系起来。实际上，虽然他认为霸权是政治（和意识形态）阶级实践领域的现象，但他也坚持认为这些必须根据国家的结构来定位。因为，虽然特定形式的国家对权力集团的组成和霸权阶级或分支的性质施加了限制，但这两者的任何变化反过来都将要求国家重组。因此，波兰察斯认为自由（或非干预主义）国家是确保竞争资本政治统治的最佳外壳，同时暗示，垄断资本必须将自由国家替换为干预主义国家（及后来的“威权主义”形式）以确保其政治统治的最佳外壳（1968年，第150-151、234、242、248、314页；1970年，第21、27、28-29、72-73、75、95、311页；1974年，第45、98、101-103、158页；1978年，第123、166-167、172、203-204页）。然而，在这些限制内，不同的资本分支完全有可能享有霸权，从而影响特定社会构成中资本主义的具体发展道路（1974年，第92-93页）。因为，除了根据CMP（资本主义生产方式）的阶段对资本进行本质分割外，资本还根据其在国家和国际资本流通中的位置而分割成不同分支。因此，波兰察斯跟随马克思和恩格斯的建议，不仅指出自由国家中的工业、商业、银行或农业资本分支可以行使霸权，还论证干预主义国家中的工业或银行资本分支可以行使霸权，并在其他地方提到了在美国导向和欧共体（EEC）导向的垄断资本分支之间的霸权转移（1968年，第232-240、302、302n、306-307、314页；1970年，第94-95、116页；1974年，第74-75、76、92-93、96、109、130-131、132-133、136页；1976b，第28-31、33、47页；1978年，第128、133、212页）。

关于“正常”与“例外”形式的讨论

这些关于政治阶级斗争和霸权的重要论点，在尼科斯·波兰察斯（Nicos Poulantzas）对“正常”和“例外”国家的分析中特别突出。对这些对比形式的国家最普遍的区别，在于前者对应于资产阶级霸权稳定与安全的结合，后者对应于霸权危机（1968年，第293页；1970年，第11、57-59、72、298、313页；1976b，第92-93页）。因此，虽然“正常”国家的共识时刻主导了宪法化暴力，但“例外”国家涉及增加物理镇压和对被统治阶级的“公开战争”（1968年，第226页；1970年，第152、316、318、330页；1976b，第9、92、129页）。反过来，这反映在这样一个事实上，即尽管具有普遍选举权和竞争政党的代表民主制机构特征“正常”国家，“例外”国家暂停选举原则（可能的例外是容易操纵的公投和/或全民公决）并消除多党制（1968年，第123、230、246-247页；1970年，第324-327页；1976b，第49、91、114页）。此外，虽然“正常”国家中的意识形态国家机器通常是私有的，因此享有相当程度的自主权脱离其控制，但“例外”国家中的机器则受到镇压性国家机器的从属，部分是为了合法化增加的强制措施，部分是为了克服伴随霸权危机的意识形态危机（1970年，第314-318页；1976b，第113-114页）。这种控制与国家机器的组织和内部运作中官僚主义的增加相匹配（1968年，第333、334-340、344-349页；1970年，第327-328、330页；1974年，第274-276页；1978年，第58-60页），以及与其分支之间权力分立的下降相匹配，这与从属分支被主导分支渗透和/或平行权力网络和传输带的扩张紧密相关，这些网络和传输带横跨并连接不同的分支（1970年，第315-316、328-329页；1976b，第50、100-101页）。这在“正常”国家的法治及其伴随的宪法限制和对权力转移的法律规制与“例外”国家至少在公共法领域的任意性（为了重组霸权领域）所采用的做法之间的对比中显而易见（1968年，第226-227、311页；1970年，第320-324页；1978年，第87-92页，但对比，1978年，第76、85页）。简而言之，如果“正常”国家依赖于在主导阶级（阶级）的霸权下稳定运作的代表民主制机构，“例外”国家则消除了民主制度和被统治阶级的自治组织，取而代之的是依靠强制措施以及一定的物质让步和意识形态攻势来确保资本的统治。

波兰察斯认为，代表民主制机构促进了基于权力集团内部以及该集团与普罗大众之间“不稳定的妥协均衡”的霸权的有机循环和重组。它因此抑制了全球资产阶级社会再生产中的重大破裂或断裂。相比之下，“例外”国家的发展是为了响应无法通过正常民主方式解决的政治和意识形态危机，重组权力集团及其与人民的关系。但它也倾向于“凝固”其构成时占主导地位的力量平衡，因此在面对新的干扰和矛盾时显示出僵硬（1976b，第30、38、48-50、90-92、93、106、124页）。最好情况下，这种形式的国家在它建立一个政治机构以集中和引导大众支持（例如，法西斯党和工会）、复制传输带和平行权力网络以促进对“黑色议会主义”的权力分配的快速改变的响应（使用格拉姆西的术语，它类似于“黑市”）以及激发一种渗透到被统治阶级以及主导阶级的意识形态，从而成为社会构成的“粘合剂”，这种情况下可以保持一定程度的灵活性（1968年，第105-106、128-129、251-256、329-330、331页；1976b，第71、83-85、124页）。最坏情况下，这样的政权与大众隔绝，缺乏专门的政治-意识形态机构来引导和控制大众支持，显示出国家权力在“宗派”、“小团体”和“封建领地”之间的僵化分割，缺乏一种能够将国家机器团结成统一集团的意识形态。这导致了对大众采取一系列不一致的政策，以努力中和他们的反对，并在权力集团内部“经济-企业”利益之间进行纯粹机械性的妥协、战术联盟和账目清算（1976b，第49-50、55-57、76、79-80、83-84、94、120-121、124-126页；参见1965c，第882-884、1050-1058页；1970年，第330、345页）。反过来，这加剧了国家机器内部的矛盾和在面对经济和/或政治危机时的僵硬性（1976b，第91、93-94、112-113、120、125-126页）。

这两种情况分别由法西斯国家和军事独裁政权所示，尽管波兰察斯没有以同样程度讨论它，波拿巴主义似乎是一个中间案例。因为，尽管波拿巴主义缺乏法西斯主义所拥有的大众党（1970年，第87、113页），实际上，它与政治舞台上党派的代表性角色下降有关，而行政主导地位上升（1968年，第320、358-359页），但它通过动员小资产阶级政治支持巩固了大众基础，并发展了一种独特的意识形态，将这种支持与权力集团的利益进行了协调（1968年，第79、107-108、180、243-244、258-260、283、286页）。此外，尽管它不是一种“正常”形式的国家，对应于霸权危机和代表性危机（同上，第302、320页），但波拿巴主义仍然显示出围绕官僚机构的统一作用所组织的明显的中心主义（同上，第158-159、261、282-283、357-358页）。然而，应该注意的是，尽管这些“例外”形式的国家之间存在重要差异，但它们都无法确保在资产阶级民主制下可能的社会力量的灵活、有机调节和霸权的循环（1976b，第124页）。因此，正如从“正常”状态到“例外”状态的转变与政治危机相一致，而不是通过连续的、线性的路径发展一样，所以从“例外”形式到“正常”形式的转变也将涉及一系列断裂和危机，而不是简单的自我转化过程（同上，第90-91、93-94、95、97、124页）。

“威权主义国家”

这些关于“例外”国家的分析也影响了波兰察斯在他最近关于“正常”国家的讨论。他建议资本主义国家的新形式是“威权主义国家”，并将其基本的发展趋势定义为“对社会经济生活各个领域加强国家控制，与政治民主制度的根本性衰退和对所谓‘形式’自由的严酷和多样形式的削减相结合”（1978年，第203-204页）。更具体地，他认为威权主义国家及其对代表民主制的含义的主要元素包括：首先，权力从立法机构转移至行政机构，以及在后者内权力的集中；其次，立法、行政和司法三个国家分支之间的加速融合，伴随着法治的衰退；第三，政治党派作为政府的特权对话者以及组织霸权的主导力量的功能性衰退；最后，平行权力网络的增长，横切国家的正式组织，对其活动具有决定性的影响（1979a，第132页；参见1976c，第55-57页；1978年，第217-231页）。"},

这些变化促进了国家的三个分支——立法机构、行政机构和司法机构——的融合，这在自由宪政国家中至少享有形式上的分离（1968年，第303-307、310-315页；1974年，第173页；1976c，第55-56页；1978年，第222-225、227-228页；1979年，第132页）。因此，虽然议会机构已成为一个仅具有非常有限权力的“登记室”，国家官僚机构正成为制定国家政策的主要行动者以及在政治行政领导下的主要场所。实际权力正在迅速集中和中央集权于政府和行政系统的高层，实际上越来越集中于总统或首相办公室——作为各种行政结构顶端，结果出现了一种个人主义的总统/首相制系统（1968年，第311-314页；1978年，第221-222、224、227-228、233、238页）。同时，党派体系和政治党派的角色也发生了重大变化。最重要的是，权力集团的党派和权力集团之间的代表性联系松动（权力集团发现通过议会的党派组织其霸权困难，转而集中于行政部门），以及党派和人民大众之间的联系松动（这种代表性越来越多通过游说系统以改良主义、经济-企业级别进行中介）（1968年，第313、313-314n、320页；1974年，第171页；1978年，第221-223页）。这些党派不再通过围绕党派计划的妥协和联盟来制定政策，并通过选举竞争获得国家-人民授权来合法化国家权力的传统功能，而是演变成为行政决策的传输带（1978年，第229页）。反过来，政治合法性的主要渠道被重新引向依赖大众媒体并由行政机构主导的全民投票和操纵技术（同上）。在当前资本主义生产方式（CMF）阶段，议会机构、法治和政治党派的衰落意味着代表民主制及其政治自由的根本衰退，以及对所有社会关系领域的威权控制的同步扩张（同上，第230-231页）。

尽管国家官僚机构成为代表垄断资本主导的权力集团利益制定国家政策的主要代理，但其活动不断遭遇其物质组织和/或其不同阶级、分支和社会类别间内部矛盾和冲突再生产的固有限制。这就提出了如何统一和同质化国家行政部门以确保其代表垄断资本有效运作的问题。在例外状态下，这是通过与行政部门不同的政治机构（如法西斯党、军队、政治警察）实现的；在理论上的正常情况下，即代表民主制中，这是通过位于中央行政机构某一距离的多党制的有机运作来实现的（1978年，第231、232-233页；参比1968年，第318-320、335-337、345-346、348、353-355页；1970年，第316-317、332、340-341、353页；1976b，第33、104-107页）。

但“威权主义国家”的情况下如何实现这一点呢？波兰察斯提出需要一个能够作为并行网络运作并确保行政部门完全政治从属于行政高层的主导大众党。这个“国家党”充当行政部门核心的政治政委，并与关键公务员形成日益增长的物质和意识形态共同体（1978年，第233-236页）。同时，这个党必须将国家意识形态传输给人民大众，并加强威权主义国家的全民投票合法性（同上，第236-237页）。尽管威权主义国家倾向于需要一个统一、结构严密的单一主导大众党，并且在政府长期不轮替的情况下最有可能实现这一点，但当一个单一的跨党派“中心”主导多党制中轮替的权力党派时，这种需求也可以得到满足（同上，第232、235-236页）。

然而，尽管在大都会资本主义国家内部威权主义国家得到了巩固，政治危机和国家危机的一般性要素还在进一步加剧。这表现在日益政治化的永久行政部门相对于支持主导的“国家党”而不是向左偏移的部分两极分化（特别是在与新小资产阶级紧密联系的低级官员中，他们在与人民大众的对峙中扮演着前线角色），行政部门内部力量关系的相对僵化，与通过有机多党制可能的灵活力量重组相比，以及新形式国家干预所引发的各种形式的大众斗争（同上，第240-247页）。简而言之，尽管威权主义国家涉及国家权力以牺牲代表民主制的方式的明确加强，它也涉及到在确保资产阶级霸权条件方面的明显削弱。这为左翼在争取向社会主义的民主过渡中提供了机遇和危险（同上，第241、263-265页）。"},

波兰察斯最初认为，资本主义涉及经济与政治领域之间的特有制度性分离，然后他补充说，经济不仅是最终决定性的（就像所有生产方式一样），而且是主导性的（在这个意义上，劳动过程和剩余劳动的占有是通过交换关系而不是经济以外的力量来调解的）。这并不意味着国家不干预经济，而是意味着其作用局限于维护资本积累的“外部”条件。因此，波兰察斯指出，法律如何通过将生产与剥削关系的法律表述作为私有财产权益，来制裁这些关系，通过合同和商业法组织流通领域，并调节对经济领域的国家干预（1970年，第322、324页；参见1968年，第53、56、163、214、228页；1974年，第100页；1978年，第39、191页）。他还论证了，法律-政治领域对经济阶级斗争具有重要影响，通过“孤立效应”。因为法律秩序将生产主体召唤为个别的法律主体，而不是对立阶级的成员：这意味着经济主体不会将资本主义关系体验为阶级关系，而是体验为相互孤立的个体和/或零散的工人和资本家群体之间的竞争关系（1968年，第130-131、213-214、275-276、310页；1978年，第63-67、69-70、86-88页）。这一效应已经对经济和政治领域的“外部性”提出了问题，事实上，在后来的自我批评中，波兰察斯承认他倾向于将这些领域视为独立且相互不可渗透的，因而无法把握国家“干预”经济的性质或作用（1976a，第18页；参见1974年，第100-101、167-168页；1978年，第17-19、26-27、166-167页）。这些问题被经常提出的观点所加剧，即垄断资本主义的增长涉及将统治力从经济领域转移到政治领域，但不改变资本主义生产方式（CMP）的基本矩阵（1968年，第55-56、91、150、211、345页；1970年，第20-21、74-75、303、313页；1974年，第42、45、81、100-101、165-168页；1978年，第166-168页）。波兰察斯最多承认，这涉及到CMP的经济和政治领域分离形式的转变，并强调，经济干预的增长仍然依赖于这两个领域的分离（1974年，第168页；1978年，第166-167、190页）。有关这种“转移”的各种论点，对波兰察斯对资本主义国家的整体划分以及对CMP本身的描述至关重要，我们现在将尽可能详细地考虑它们。

让我们首先回顾两个论点。首先，波兰察斯表示，随着雇佣劳动在资本主义控制下的“实质性归属”，出现了CMP的典型矩阵。这发生在大规模工业或机器制造业的兴起时期（而不是基于制造业的简单合作），并与资本的整个循环由生产资本的周期决定（与制造业过渡期的商业或商品资本相对立） （1968年，第32、127、159页；1974年，第96页；参见马克思，1867年，第312-315、578页）。其次，波兰察斯论证，在纯粹的CMP中，所有资本主义剥削的基础是剩余价值的创造和占有（1968年，第32、129页；1970年，第304页；1974年，第19、53、63、92、95-96、116、132、211-213、221页；1978年，第17、18页）。
